newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-PNZ sees room for another profit leap.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-PNZ sees room for another profit leap.

text.p: Power New Zealand Ltd chief executive Doug Heffernan said on Thursday the Auckland power distributor had potential to match 1996/7's 20 percent profit increase in the current year to March 1998.

"There is certainly the potential to have the same level of profit lift in the year ahead, particularly with the ability now to sit down and talk about things on a commercial basis with Mercury, which in the past has been off limits because they've all been wrapped up in the share battle," Heffernan said.
"So if you roll those in and look at the overall level of efficiencies that are available within the industry, I think the prospects for Power NZ shareholders are really good," he said.

"The more you look towards cooperation and commercial relationships with Mercury on generation or in terms of things with (state power grid) Trans Power, maybe there is more than that available," he told Reuters.
Heffernan said an increase in net profit of the same magnitude as 1996/7 would be "right at the top end".

After years of wrangling over the control of Power NZ, major shareholders UtiliCorp United and unlisted Mercury Energy have agreed to form a joint 50/50 venture to hold their stakes and to launch a bid at NZ$6.00 for minorities.
A big chunk of Power NZ's profit comes from its network and Power NZ was one of the first to put in organised asset management regimes, which had delivered benefits.
While new power generation prospects would be evaluated, Heffernan saw opportunities to lock in attractive long term deals with state power generators ECNZ and Contact Energy.
ECNZ, Contact and new entrants were anxious to secure market share and if contracts looked attractive, Power NZ would go down that route rather than locking up cash in power generation.
The last few years had seen much in the way of organic growth plus "off-network" business outside Power NZ's area.
Power NZ has the most off-network sites while neighbouring Mercury has the most by volume.
Power NZ's Rotokawa power project, due for commissioning in July, would also contribute to net profit bottom line in the current year.
Power NZ had in the past scored some "easy" runs through its 53 percent ownership of Bay of Plenty Electricity by removing duplication in areas like generation development and off-network retailing.
"The next tier of things is really looking at trying to reduce duplication in our information and financial systems. That will be the focus in the year ahead," he said.
BOP Electricity had driven much of the 20 percent increase in pre-abnormal profit to NZ$55.32 million in the March year but Heffernan did not foresee other such acquisitions.
Pacific Energy's 37.5 percent equity accounted contribution fell to NZ$250,000 from just under $5.0 million a year earlier, when Power NZ's share was 50 percent.
The decline in Pacific's profitability was a reflection of the conservative approach the owners had to the power trader's risk management, he said.
